title: Theme or Topic?
summary: One cluster of coded extracts and four candidate statements about it, sorted one at a time into a topic summary, a staging post, a developed theme, or something the data cannot carry.
learningObjectives: Distinguish a topic summary from a developed theme.
Recognise a true, supported, descriptive sentence as a stage in an analysis rather than a theme.
Identify the organising concept that makes a theme analytic.
Identify a statement that overreaches, and say which feature of the design it exceeds.
Explain why a label everything fits under is not organising anything.
interactionTypes: four-way classification of one candidate at a time
a fixed category order so the answer position varies rather than being learnable
no elimination, because each candidate is judged before the next is seen
privacy: Nothing is collected, stored or transmitted.
accessibilityNotes: Keyboard operable throughout. Answered options are marked aria-disabled rather than disabled so they stay in the tab order and can be re-read, and each state carries a glyph and a visually hidden sentence as well as a colour. The cluster of codes and quotes stays on screen throughout. No timed content and no motion.
dataStatus: Fictional. The extracts are invented for teaching and no participant, interview, institution or study is represented.
simulationNotes: Four categories is a teaching simplification: real candidate themes sit on a continuum and several of these could be argued into a neighbouring category by a good supervisor. The developed theme offered is defensible rather than uniquely correct, and other themes built around other organising concepts would also work. The three overreaching failures in the full version fail in three different ways; the one kept here asserts a cause an interview study cannot establish and is also contradicted by the data.
readmeTopic: topics, staging posts, themes and overreach in qualitative analysis
